newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - EU pins competitive hopes on enlargement, EMU.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - EU pins competitive hopes on enlargement, EMU.

text.p: European hopes are running high that the single currency and eastern enlargement will help boost the competitive power of the continent's industry which lags behind that of its rival economic superpower, the United States.
Economic and monetary union (EMU) and the accession of former communist countries to the now 15-nation European Union are likely to speed up needed but painful restructuring.
Over time, leaner and more efficient industries would be better equipped to challenge U.S. and Japanese competitors.
But there could also be considerable pain as industries, regions and workers are forced to adjust to an increasingly competitive and specialised economic environment.
"There is going to be a lot more consolidation, rationalisation taking place and that is what we need," said Vicky Pryce, chief economist at KPMG Management Consulting.
"The only problem is that the transition costs are horrendously high," she added. "The cost in terms of short-term unemployment is rather high."
Although not directly linked, EMU and enlargement are both expected to have major impacts on an EU economy plagued by high unemployment, with 18 million of its 370 million people out of work.
"They are both very positive," said Keith Richardson, secretary general of the European Round Table of Industrialists, a Brussels-based body grouping European company leaders.
He noted that EMU would have an immediate impact while enlargement would take longer to affect the EU economy.
By both deepening and widening the single market -- launched on January 1, 1993 -- EMU and enlargement should lead to further industry specialisation and relocation as competition hots up.
"What it will do up to a point is displace what is going on in Europe and we are going to find countries specialising a lot more in things they are good at," said Pryce.
"There will be a shake-out, in my view, in a number of places and the employment levels we've seen in some countries will probably even increase."
ENLARGEMENT WOULD ADD 100 MILLION CONSUMERS IN THE EU

Expansion across the former Iron Curtain to 10 applicant central and eastern European countries would bring more than 100 million consumers as well as a skilled and cheap workforce into the EU, already the world's largest internal market.

"Enlargement to central and eastern Europe should benefit EU industry as a result of the expected increase in economic activity," the European Commission said in a document on enlargement published in July.
"Better allocation of resources will strengthen its competitiveness in the global economy."

If all applicant countries were to join now, the number of EU citizens would increase by 30 percent to almost half a billion but gross domestic product would grow by only five percent, a sign of the wide gap in wealth and development.
The average GDP per inhabitant in the applicant states is just one third of the EU level, but the growth rates of these countries are often higher.

Rewarding those which have made most progress, the Commission recommended in July that the EU should start membership talks in early 1998 with five of the applicants -- the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Poland and Slovenia.

The euro, on the other hand, would remove currency-related barriers to trade and help improve the functioning of the single market, in which goods, people, services and capital are supposed to move freely across national borders.
Advocates also say EMU will reduce transaction costs and currency uncertainty.
"Markets are still fragmented due to different currencies," said economist Peter Vanden Houte at Bank Brussels Lambert (BBL).
Daniel Gros, senior research fellow at the Centre for European Policy Studies in Brussels, predicted EMU would lower interest rates and encourage investments and industry productivity.
EUROPE NEEDS AN ECONOMIC BOOST
Europe, lagging behind the United States in terms of job creation, employment rates and productivity levels, is in need of an economic shot in the arm.
Commission figures show that the EU has managed to create only 10 million new jobs since the 1960s, less than one fifth of the number in the United States.
As a result, the EU unemployment rate stands at 11 percent compared with about five percent in the United States.
EU gross domestic product per capita is nearly one third below that of the United States.
There are hopes that EMU and enlargement will help improve the situation, but no one pretends it will be easy.
While stressing the positive effects, the Commission said that enlargement would put major adjustment pressure on some sectors.

"Sensitive areas for the Union as a whole could include the labour market, although alarmist forecasts would not seem justified, certain industries, especially in labour intensive and other traditional sectors, some areas of transport etc."
Such tensions could give rise to protectionist reactions, in both new and present member states, it added.

Western firms may move more production plants to eastern Europe to take advantage of lower costs, which would be good for their competitiveness but could cause problems for the areas in western Europe where plants were closed.

"Through this process of specialisation, the labour-intensive part of European industry will come under pressure and the rest will become more competitive," said Gros at CEPS. "That shift is happening and will happen more."
EURO WOULD IMPROVE PRICE COMPARISONS

The planned launch of the euro in 1999 is also expected to intensify competition, increase transparency and make it easier for consumers to compare prices. Today, for example, the price of the same car model may vary widely in the EU.
"Competition between market participants will become fiercer since the situation will no longer be obscured by different currencies," Deutsche Bank Research wrote in a recent paper.

BBL's Vanden Houte noted that there had already been one major industry consolidation phase around the time that the single market was consolidated in the late 1980s and early 1990s, and predicted that EMU would lead to a second wave.
He cited the financial sector, currently one of the EU's more fragmented industries. "There consolidation will definitely be very important in coming years," he said.

Companies will face increased competitive pressure, but also greater opportunities. "It is important that they see the integration of their domestic and foreign markets as a chance to widen their sphere of activity, and ultimately to increase their profits," Deutsche Bank Research said.

By removing the ability to devalue currencies to restore competitiveness, EMU may also force governments to undertake reforms to make labour markets more flexible, seen as crucial for Europe to reduce record joblessness. "EMU is going to be a big trigger in the process," said Vanden Houte.
